newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan markets view election with jaded eyes.
newsitem.headline: Japan markets view election with jaded eyes.

text.p: Japan's upcoming general election may be touted by political leaders as a "turning point", but Japanese financial markets are responding like the nation's voters -- with apathy and uncertainty.
"There won't be much impact. It's always the same group of people, so they're not really going to change anything," said Sidney Hui, vice president and chief dealer at Bank of America in Tokyo.
The main question for markets about the October 20 polls is whether the long-ruling conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) can win a majority or Japan will again be governed by a coalition.
"Until we can paint a clearer picture of a new government, we (the stock market) won't be able to move much," said Tadahiro Kamogawa, senior analyst at Yamaichi Securities.
Private polls show there is only a slim chance of any party winning an outright majority.

Adding to this unpredictability is an expected record low voter turnout. More than half the Japanese electorate say they have no idea whom to support and a similar number are confused by a complex new electoral system.
The uncertainty of the election's outcome has been casting a pall over the Tokyo stock market for days, inhibiting trade.

Kaoru Ichikawa, a senior trader at Kokusai Securities, said it might not make much difference which party leads the government in the event of a coalition, but that the confusing outlook has made investors cautious.

A recent survey by the financial daily Nikkei Kinyu Shimbun revealed many stock market analysts want the pro-business LDP to regain the majority it held for nearly four decades prior to the 1993 election, as time-consuming debate among coalition partners in recent years may have delayed crucial decisions to bolster the flagging economy.
Others, however, feel that even a resounding victory by the LDP -- traditionally seen as good for business -- is unlikely to give markets much joy.

"Even if we get results with a robust showing for the LDP...the LDP is perceived as a conservative force. The (currency) market is not looking for business-as-usual policies, but more radical deregulation," said Andrew Shipley, an economist at Schroders Securities.

Noting that the LDP's shock fall from power in 1993 sparked no response from the foreign exchange market, he added: "Political...uncertainty depressed the currency market reaction and we will see the same thing this time."
Kenneth Landon, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said an LDP win would be a renewal of the status quo and hence would have little impact on currencies.
Most scenarios besides that of an LDP majority win would suggest to markets that interest rates might rise, but the impact of that would be more psychological than real, he said.

"This (sentiment) could see quick selling of a lot of dollar positions against the yen, but setbacks are temporary at best, maybe to around 109.80 yen," Landon added. The dollar was trading at around 111.35 yen in Tokyo trade on Friday.

A victory by the main opposition Shinshinto is seen as a high-risk scenario by the bond market. Shinshinto is pledging huge tax cuts, which dealers say would depress bond prices for two reasons -- this would boost consumption and spark inflation, and force the government to issue new bonds to make up for drops in tax revenue thus swamping the bond market.

"Various polls indicate the LDP will lead, but in the past, the Shinshinto has done better in the actual election than private polls forecast, so I'm really vigilant about the possibility of Shinshinto's gaining," said Katsuzo Sakamoto, general manager of Daiwa Securities' bond & finance division.
